edges.effect_quant: The strongest evidence shows that oral-contraceptive use is associated with a meaningful reduction in endometrial-cancer risk, with longer use producing larger protection that persists for years after stopping.
edges.mechanism: Combined oral contraceptives reduce endometrial proliferation by providing progestogenic opposition to estrogen-driven growth and by suppressing ovulation-related hormonal cycling. That mechanism fits the dose-duration pattern seen in epidemiology, where longer exposure is linked to stronger risk reduction.
edges.summary: This is one of the clearer protective associations in reproductive epidemiology. Large pooled analyses and newer meta-analyses consistently show that oral-contraceptive use lowers endometrial-cancer risk, with the most durable benefit seen after several years of use.
edges.caveats: Risk reduction is relative to baseline endometrial-cancer risk and should not be generalized to every hormonal formulation or every patient context. Any counseling still has to weigh this benefit against other oral-contraceptive tradeoffs, including small increases in some other hormone-sensitive cancers.
